THE VICTORVILLE PROTOCOL

Major Jonathan Spencer set down his regulation fork beside the bulletproof glass of water that sat on every table in the officers' mess at Forward Operating Base Glendale. The war had been over for three months, but certain precautions remained.

"Isn't that Colonel Henry Martin at that table?" he heard himself say.

Lieutenant Samuel James, seated across from him, looked uncomfortable without actually turning around. "Not at all. Somebody who looks like him. You know how it is. Martin's dead, don't you remember? KIA at Shadowbrook."

Spencer remembered. James had to know that he would remember. They had served together in the same battalion. What were they trying to pull on him? "The man who isn't Martin is leaving," Spencer said, describing the scene over James's shoulder. "If that's Martin's brother, I might catch him to pay my respects."

"No," James said quickly, "I wouldn't do that."

"Martin came to my wife's memorial service before deployment. It's the least I could do."

"I wouldn't. Probably no relation to Martin at all. Somebody who looks like him."

"He's practically running," Spencer said. "He almost ran out of the mess hall."

"Who? Oh, the man who looked like Martin, you mean."

"Yes," Spencer said.

A thick-bodied man at the next table, wearing civilian contractor credentials, leaned back against Spencer's chair.

"That fellow who just left looked like a friend of yours, huh?" the thick man said.

"Couldn't have been him, though," Spencer answered automatically. "My friend's dead. Killed in action."

The thick man rocked forward and stood abruptly. He threw cash on the table as if disgusted with it and walked out quickly.

James breathed in deeply. "Now you've probably got old Martin into trouble."

"Martin's dead," Spencer said.

"Oh, well, 'dead,'" James replied with strange emphasis.

"What do you say it like that for?" Spencer demanded angrily. "The man's dead. KIA. There's no doubt about it. I saw the casualty report myself."

"You know how it is," James said vaguely.

Spencer had thought he understood death. He had lost three men under his command in the Battle of Brookhaven. He had watched Anna Burns, his wife, waste away from the disease before he deployed. He had known what he believed to be genuine grief. Even after they had transferred him to the psychiatric ward at Victorville for combat stress and released him as recovered, he still believed he understood death. But apparently he didn't understand it at all.

Linton felt that his silence was asking James by this time.

"I don't know, mind you," James said, lowering his voice, "but I suppose he might have been through the Victorville Protocol."

"What protocol?" Spencer asked, thinking: What the hell is he talking about?

"The military resurrection program. Who knows who authorized it? Probably buried in some black budget."

"You mean somebody has invented a way to bring dead soldiers back to life?" Spencer said flatly.

He knew, of course, that James probably didn't mean literal resurrection. James probably meant some kind of identity theft or records manipulation. But by saying something so ridiculous, Spencer hoped to force the truth out immediately.

"An invention? I guess that's what it is," James agreed. "Nanotechnology, mostly. Cellular reconstruction. I don't know much about it. I'm just a line officer."

"But it's incredible," Spencer said, his mind racing. "Incredible! Why would something like that be classified? Why don't more people know about it?"

"Sh-h," James said uneasily. "This is a public place."

"I don't understand," Spencer said.

"Look, Jonathan, you can't just legalize military resurrection," James said with forced patience. "There are massive organizational behavior issues to consider. Chain of command gets complicated when people come back. Who outranks who? What about promotions given after someone died? The Veterans Affairs has a lobby. Death benefits, life insurance, survivor pensions—it's their whole bureaucratic existence. You've got to realize that."

"That's not enough. Not nearly enough reason to keep it secret."

"Think of all the problems it would cause. Medal of Honor recipients who died heroically—do you take back their medals if they're resurrected? What about unit cohesion when half your squad has died and come back? The psychological impact on decision-making in combat situations. And the enemy—if they find out we can resurrect soldiers, what does that do to deterrence theory?"

"But what do they do about it? How does it work?"

"There are experimental facilities. When the brass finds out about unauthorized resurrections, they shut them down, destroy the equipment, court-martial everybody involved. That's about all they can do. The charges usually fall under unauthorized use of classified technology."

"I don't understand," Spencer complained. "Why haven't I heard about this?"

"They didn't talk about shell shock in World War One either, not officially. There was an article I read that said 'death' was our military's unspoken word, not casualties or losses. You want to shock a general, you tell him straight out, 'Your soldiers are going to be dead,' not 'KIA' or 'fallen.' You know how it is. The opposite of 'alive' these days is 'administratively processed.'"

"I see," Spencer said.

He tried to process it. Of course, he had been out of the loop for some time during his psychiatric treatment. It might be true. Then again, they might be testing him to see if he was really stable. But the possibility was too compelling.

"Tell me, Samuel, where could I find someone who knows about the Victorville Protocol?"

James looked away. "Jonathan, I don't have anything to do with that kind of operation, and if you're smart, you won't either."

Spencer's fist hit the table. "Damn you, James, you tell me!"

James stood up quickly. "I bring you to dinner to help you reintegrate after your psychiatric discharge, to make you feel welcome back among your fellow officers. I do all that, and for thanks, you yell at me and curse me. You PTSD cases are all alike!"

James threw money on the table and stalked out.

I've got to hurry, Spencer thought. If Martin's alive, maybe Anna could be too.

---

The doctor fluttered around the underground facility. "Well, well, Major Spencer, we understand you've been causing disturbances."

"Not really," Spencer said from the chair where two MPs had deposited him.

"Come, come," the doctor chided. "You broke into a restricted area of the base, assaulted a guard, demanded access to classified files. That's disturbing, Major, very disturbing."

"I was only trying to find out something," Spencer maintained. "They could have told me. Everyone seems to know but me."

The doctor made a dismissive sound. "Let's not think any such thing. Most people don't know about the Victorville Protocol."

Spencer rubbed his shoulder where the guard had struck him. "That guard knew more combat techniques than I did."

"A few specific people know a few specific things you don't. But let me ask you, Major, could Einstein plan a military campaign?"

"I don't know. Who the hell ever wasted Einstein's time asking him that?"

"People who want answers have to ask the right questions. You can find out anything by asking the right person at the right time."

Spencer stared suspiciously. "Do you work on the Victorville Protocol?"

"I am the Victorville Protocol. I designed it."

"But the MPs brought me to you!"

"Well, that's what needed to happen, wasn't it? Did you think MPs would just arrest you for nothing? Cynics—all you combat veterans are cynics."

Spencer leaned forward on the uncomfortable metal chair and really looked at the doctor for the first time. The man wore civilian clothes but had a military bearing. Behind him, through reinforced glass, Spencer could see laboratory equipment that looked like something from a science fiction novel—nanite tanks bubbling with amber fluid, cellular reconstruction chambers humming with power. One workstation held what appeared to be scientific instruments for examining samples at high magnification. Glass bottles of various solutions lined the shelves in precise rows, some filled with amber reagents, others containing cultures that seemed to pulse with bioluminescent activity.

"Doctor, can you really resurrect the dead?"

"Will you stop being cynical? Of course I can. That's what the Victorville Protocol is."

"Doctor, I'm beginning to believe you," Spencer said, "but tell me, can you resurrect someone who's been dead a long time?"

"Duration has minimal impact on the process."

"My wife has been dead for over a year. She died before I deployed."

"A year?" The doctor snapped his fingers. "It could be years. Decades, theoretically. It's all nanotechnology and cellular reconstruction, Major. I need only one fragment of tissue and my computers can map the complete genetic structure and rebuild it. The neural patterns are more complex—we use statistical inference from personality profiles, service records, educational background. It's remarkably accurate. Naturally, there is some degree of risk involved."

"Accurate risk," Spencer murmured. "Could you start right away?"

"First, we must discuss resources. This isn't a sanctioned military operation. It requires significant funding."

Spencer grasped the situation immediately. "You want money. You realize I'm just a major's salary..."

"I've worked with various compensation structures."

"I don't have much," Spencer said. "Most of my savings went to Anna's medical bills before she died."

"Then—"

"But I have my death benefit insurance. I could sign it over to you. And I have some investments. Not much, but it's all I have."

"That might be sufficient," the doctor said, calculating. "Now we must obtain tissue samples. You said your wife—Anna, was it?—has been deceased for over a year?"

"Yes. She's buried in Brookhaven, Relvaria."

The doctor nodded. "We'll need to exhume the body. I have contacts who can handle the paperwork. The resurrection process takes approximately seventy-two hours once we have viable tissue."

Spencer felt his heart racing. "Doctor, my mind is spinning. I never thought this was possible."

The doctor smiled thinly. "The impossible is just the improbable that hasn't been funded yet."

---

The exhumation permit had been easier to obtain than Spencer expected. The doctor had taken tissue samples and Spencer's entire financial future and fed them into the maw of his computers. Through nanotechnology and cellular reconstruction, through statistical inference and neural mapping, Anna would be reborn.

Spencer shook his head. It seemed impossible. But then Anna opened the heavy steel door of the doctor's laboratory and walked out into the harsh fluorescent lighting.

It wasn't fair, Spencer thought. He should have had time to prepare himself.

Anna lifted her arms, stretching. "Jonathan!" she said.

"Anna!" he said, feeling a slight wrongness but suppressing it. No doubt he would adjust to her having been dead the same way he had learned to accept her illness.

Anna crossed the room and embraced him. She kissed his cheek. "It's so wonderful to be back. This calls for a celebration. We must see Timothy, Layla, all our old friends."

"Yes," he said, his heart sinking at her ignorance. "But tell me—how was it being... away?"

Her body tensed against his. Her expression changed.

"I can't remember," she said. "I can't really remember anything clearly. My memories feel like someone else's memories, like literary criticism of a book I never read..."

"Now, now," Spencer said, "we mustn't get upset. You've been through an ordeal."

She accepted this. She pulled away and touched her hair. It was the same hair, dark brown and straight. Of course it would be; the nanotechnology would have reconstructed it perfectly from the genetic template.

"I must see all our old friends," Anna persisted. "Layla and Timothy..."

"My darling," he said gently, "about Timothy—"

Her eyes widened. "Yes? What about Timothy Kelly?"

"It was a combat situation. About six months ago. He was killed. IED in Shadowbrook, Marvenia."

"Killed?" Anna repeated. "Timothy was killed?"

"Died instantly. He didn't suffer."

"But Timothy was your friend, your best friend from basic training. Why didn't you have him resurrected the same way you did me?"

"Darling, the Victorville Protocol is experimental and expensive. You have to pay premium prices for renewable energy in a desert. I no longer have the resources to pay for Timothy's resurrection."

Anna turned her back to him. "It's just as well. You shouldn't bring Timothy back to this half-life, give him reconstructed memories and a simulated soul. It's wrong. No one should do this. But you're sure you don't have the resources?"

"No," Spencer said. "I'm bankrupt. I've signed over everything. My death benefit won't pay out until I'm dead, and then, of course, you could resurrect me."

"Of course," Anna said. She sighed. "Poor Timothy. He was such a good friend. You must miss him. I'm so sorry."

"I have you," he said simply.

"Jonathan," she said, her voice suddenly flat, "you should see that laboratory. There are nanite tanks, cellular reconstruction chambers, neural mapping equipment, waste reduction systems for failed experiments. It's perfect."

"It sounds disturbing," he said uneasily.

"No, dear, it's perfect for what needs to be done."

Anna walked toward the doctor's workstation. Spencer watched her move through the laboratory, her fingers trailing along the equipment. She paused at the shelf of glass bottles, lifting one filled with amber liquid to examine it against the light. The bottle was substantial—thick laboratory glass, perhaps a liter in volume. She seemed to weigh it in her hand before setting it back among the others.

"These reagents," she murmured. "Essential for the resurrection process, I assume."

She moved on to examine the examination equipment on its heavy brass stand. The instrument gleamed under the fluorescent lights, its multiple adjustment knobs and viewing apparatus marking it as precision scientific equipment.

"This is remarkable," she said, touching the brass fittings. "The precision required for cellular mapping. Do you know how it works?"

"Anna, I don't care about the equipment. I care about you."

Her eyes flashed around the doctor's office, calculating distances. Spencer noticed she had positioned herself between him and the door.

"Jonathan, I'm sorry," she said. "But I need that death benefit. I need to live. Don't you understand? This isn't life!"

She moved with terrible speed. Spencer saw her hands close around something heavy, saw her pivot toward him, saw the object raised high. He threw himself sideways as she swung, and the blow struck the shelf behind where he'd stood. Glass shattered—bottles exploding, amber solution spraying across the floor. The impact knocked something loose from her grip, and she scrambled to recover her weapon from among the debris.

Malfunction, he concluded. Neural mapping error. Personality reconstruction failure.

She raised the object again, dripping with solution from where it had struck through the bottles, and he caught her wrists. She struggled against him, the weight straining both their arms—the thing must have weighed at least fifteen pounds, all metal fittings. "I need resources to continue existing! The maintenance, the energy costs—you don't understand what it takes to keep this body functioning!"

Spencer understood immediately. He felt foolish, betrayed. All that money, all that hope. He had resurrected something that wasn't really Anna, just a simulation based on statistical inference and personality profiles.

Spencer twisted the heavy object away from his wife. The brass was cold in his hands, solid and unyielding—scientific equipment repurposed for violence. He could see his own distorted reflection in one of its glass lenses as he brought it up. She had grabbed it from its stand on that workstation, the same instrument she'd been examining moments before, the one used to map her cellular structure at the microscopic level. It would now end her reconstructed existence.

He watched her face register horror as he brought it down toward her.

He struck her down and watched her collapse amid the broken glass and spreading liquid.

Spencer was shocked by the fine metallic mesh just below the synthetic skin and those tiny components that looked like integrated circuits in the wound. No blood—just sparking filaments and the clean edges of manufactured materials.

He knelt beside the body and examined the damage, careful to avoid the glass shards surrounding them. His hands were still wrapped around the viewing instrument's brass barrel, sticky with reagent solution.

Yes, it seemed they had to use artificial components in resurrection. They couldn't truly revive the dead, just create sophisticated androids based on genetic and psychological profiles.

Or—

Did they use the original bodies at all? What were all those waste reduction systems for if the bodies were reconstructed? Didn't the resurrectionists just dispose of the corpses and build synthetic replacements?

But it didn't matter. Not really.

She had thought she was Anna, sharing her perspective down to the finest detail, and he had thought she was Anna.

It was what you believed was real that made it real, not objective truth. That was the fundamental epistemology of the Victorville Protocol.

"I've killed my wife!" Spencer called out, rising from his knees, reaching toward something beyond the room.

The pain stung him into unconsciousness—a sharp pain in his neck like an injection, like a doorway opening into darkness.

---

He opened his eyes to the doctor's office. The doctor looked down at him with professional sympathy. "You'll have to go back to psychiatric treatment, Major Spencer. But they'll help you. You'll undergo therapy until you no longer believe your wife was resurrected or that you killed her again. Personal growth through structured intervention."

"Do you really think so, Doctor?" Spencer asked hopefully.

"I know so. The mind is remarkably resilient. You'll forget this ever happened. You'll accept that Anna died, that the Victorville Protocol was just a stress-induced delusion. You'll return to duty eventually."

"And the Protocol? Does it really exist?"

The doctor smiled enigmatically. "Does it matter? If you believe something exists, if it affects your decision-making and behavior, isn't that a form of existence? That's the real question, Major. Not what's real, but what difference reality makes."

Spencer closed his eyes. Around him, he could hear the hum of machinery, the whisper of ventilation systems, the distant sound of military operations continuing as they always had.

In Victorville, in Thandor, in all the secret facilities scattered across Glendale Province and beyond, the work continued. Soldiers died and were resurrected, or perhaps just replaced. The organizational behavior implications rippled through the military structure. Education reform was proposed to prepare soldiers for a world where death might not be permanent. Existential questions multiplied like cells in a nanite tank.

And Major Jonathan Spencer, veteran of Brookhaven and Shadowbrook, husband of the deceased Anna Burns, friend of the fallen Timothy Kelly and Henry Martin, closed his eyes and wondered what was real.

The answer, he suspected, was that reality was whatever the military said it was.

And that was the most terrifying truth of all.
